A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QuestA, with matching research identity and substantial shared content. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original QuestA training experiments, mathematical and cross-domain evaluations, and training-dynamics analyses in Tables 2–4 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations and additional controlled experiments testing prompt difficulty, hints, and curriculum design, including Tables 1, 3, and 5.

M1.justification: v2 uses fixed 50% hints and describes curriculum training as future work. v3 implements a 50%-to-25% curriculum and adds difficulty filtering after augmentation at each stage (Section 3, Appendix A.5). These substantially extend the training procedure; the underlying GRPO objective and reward remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both retain OpenR1-Math-220K and OpenMathReasoning, the same five mathematical benchmarks, and GPQA Diamond, Zebralogic, Code Contests, Codeforces, and LiveCodeBench V5. Cross-domain results move to v3 Appendix C.2. New difficulty splits and smaller training subsets change sampling within existing coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Easy-Nemotron and Hard-Nemotron RL comparators (Figures 2 and 17), plus a same-data RL comparator without hints (Table 5). These provide substantial comparisons absent from v2. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, included in v2 Table 2, is removed; DeepScaleR's own before/after comparison remains in v3 Table 6.

E3.justification: The main Nemotron training budget changes from 500 steps to 2,000, allocated as 100 steps with 50% hints and 1,900 with 25% hints. Additional filtering reduces the augmented pool from 26K to at most 10K problems. New easy/hard controls use approximately 4K questions each and 1,000 steps. Core benchmark decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds controlled analyses of easy versus hard training prompts, training with versus without hints, fixed 50% hints versus the two-stage curriculum, and extension to zero hints (Section 2, Section 5.2, Appendix C). The existing dataset ablation remains, with its OpenR1 comparison updated to the new fixed-50% run.

E5.justification: Both report pass@1 averaged over 32 completions and retain the same unbiased pass@k estimator and sampling condition in Appendix A.2. Neither introduces training-run repetitions, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new variance-based data selection concerns training design, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main Nemotron scores change from 67.08/59.50/35.52 to 72.50/62.29/41.67 on AIME24/AIME25/HMMT, and the five-benchmark average changes from 59.01 to 63.26 (v2 Table 2; v3 Table 1). These results use revised training conditions. v3 also adds control and curriculum results and updates training-set success and unsolved-problem findings. DeepScaleR and cross-domain table values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 removes the 'LLM as Infinite Monkey' proposition and its appendix proof. The central capacity definitions, null-gradient assumption, sampling bounds, and tabular policy-gradient proof remain substantively unchanged. The hinted-sampling lemma leaves the main text but remains in Appendix B.1.

C1.justification: v3 makes dependence of reasoning-capacity changes on training-data difficulty a principal contribution and presents an implemented curriculum as central to QuestA. v2 principally claims that fixed partial-solution augmentation expands capacity. The overall state-of-the-art and sample-efficiency claims remain, with revised headline results.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking easy-prompt RL to shallow-pattern overfitting, decreasing hints to training–evaluation alignment, and no-hint training to neglect of the hardest problems (Sections 2, 5.2, C.1). It qualifies OpenMathReasoning experiments as first-stage-only. Section 5.1 also strengthens the 32B comparison to superiority on every benchmark, although Table 1 contradicts this on AIME24.

D1.justification: v3 newly states access to code, data, and models through a project repository; its availability is not independently verified here. It supplies post-augmentation filtering thresholds, easy/hard selection rules, and exact curriculum budgets. Existing optimizer and decoding details largely persist, although v2's explicit identification of the DeepScaleR comparison baseline as Stage 3 is omitted.

R1.justification: v3 adds Gao et al.'s 'One-shot entropy minimization' and Wang et al.'s work on RL with one training example to motivate sample selection, and removes the infinite-monkey reference. The broader related-work discussion and positioning against approaches such as StepHint remain substantially intact in Appendix A.3.

P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten, and a new difficulty-versus-efficiency section reorganizes the argument. Related work, benchmark descriptions, and much DeepScaleR discussion move into expanded appendices. Citation style, author presentation, headings, and appendix organization also change substantially.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes its displayed model series, and the original four-panel pass@k presentation is reorganized into controlled comparisons and separate appendix plots. The main mathematical table is split, training plots are redrawn with revised colors, legends, and panel ordering, and new ablation tables and figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important weakness in v2: comparisons against initial checkpoints did not isolate hints from continued RL training. The same-data/schedule no-hint control and equal-2,000-step curriculum ablation directly test these contributions (Tables 5 and 3: average 63.26 versus 60.44 and 60.26). Added filtering and schedule details also improve reproducibility. These substantial evidential gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including the incorrect all-benchmark 32B comparison and Figure 5's description of entropy as increasing despite its decline after an early peak.
